cards.title: What is an Employer Identification Number (EIN)?
content: An EIN is a unique nine-digit number assigned by the IRS to identify your business for tax reporting, banking, and other legal purposes (like hiring employees).

cards.title: Do I need an EIN for my business?
content: Most US businesses need an EIN for tax reporting, opening bank accounts, and hiring employees. Sole proprietorships without employees can use the owner's Social Security Number (SSN) for tax purposes; however, even they may choose to have an EIN for several benefits like keeping their personal and business taxes separate and ensuring that their personal SSN is not being overly used, which could increase the risk of identity theft.

cards.title: How long does it take to obtain an EIN?
content: The EIN application process typically takes between 4-6 weeks. With Incorporate Wise's expedited service, you can have your EIN in 2-4 weeks after the application is made.

cards.title: Can non-US residents obtain an EIN?
content: Yes, non-US residents can obtain an EIN for their US-based businesses. Incorporate Wise can guide you through the process and ensure a successful application.

cards.title: Can I use my Social Security Number (SSN) instead of an EIN?
content: Some sole proprietors without employees may use their SSNs for tax reporting. However, obtaining an EIN is generally recommended even for them, as it separates personal and business finances and offers enhanced privacy.

cards.title: What is an ITIN?
content: An ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number) is a tax processing number issued by the IRS to individuals who are required to have a US taxpayer identification number but are not eligible for a Social Security Number (SSN). ITINs are used for tax purposes only - they don't authorize work in the US or grant social security benefits.

cards.title: When is an ITIN necessary?
content: An ITIN is needed mainly for tax filing and reporting requirements. Common cases include filing US tax returns without an SSN, claiming tax benefits or refunds, and opening a PayPal or US bank account or applying for loans where a financial institution requires one.

cards.title: What is the difference between an SSN, EIN, or ITIN?
content: All three are US tax identification numbers serving different purposes. An SSN is for US citizens and residents, an EIN identifies US business entities, and an ITIN is for individuals who need to file US taxes but are not eligible for an SSN.

cards.title: How long does it take to obtain an ITIN?
content: Processing an ITIN application typically takes 6 to 11 weeks, depending on the time of year, the completeness and accuracy of the application, and the IRS workload.

cards.title: What is a Certificate of Good Standing?
content: A Certificate of Good Standing is an official document issued by a state agency that verifies a business entity is compliant with all state requirements, including filing annual reports and paying necessary fees. It is often required for various business activities like securing financing or registering to do business in another state.

cards.title: Why might I need a Certificate of Good Standing?
content: You might need a Certificate of Good Standing to assure potential business partners, lenders, or government institutions that your company is legally authorized to conduct business and is current with state regulations. It is particularly important when applying for loans, renewing licenses, or expanding your business to additional states.

cards.title: How can I obtain a Certificate of Good Standing?
content: Obtaining a Certificate of Good Standing usually involves submitting a formal request to the relevant state agency, commonly the Secretary of State's office, along with payment of a fee. Some states offer online applications while others may require paper forms.

cards.title: How long is a Certificate of Good Standing valid?
content: The validity period of a Certificate of Good Standing varies by state and the specific requirements of the receiving entity. Some institutions may require a certificate that is dated within the last 30-60 days, while others may accept older certificates. Always check the specific requirements of the party requesting the document.

cards.title: What happens if my business is not in good standing?
content: If your business is not in good standing, it means you may have failed to meet certain state requirements, such as filing necessary documentation or paying certain taxes or fees. This can lead to penalties, loss of business rights, or the inability to obtain a Certificate of Good Standing until compliance is restored.

cards.title: Can a Certificate of Good Standing be used internationally?
content: While a Certificate of Good Standing is primarily a document for domestic business verification, it can be used internationally to demonstrate compliance and good standing in your home country. However, additional documentation or translation may be required depending on the foreign jurisdiction's requirements.

cards.title: What is company dissolution?
content: Company dissolution refers to the formal bureaucracy of closing a business entity. This process involves legally ending the company's existence at the state level where it's registered, and with the federal government, typically before the IRS.

cards.title: Why is dissolution necessary for a U.S. company?
content: Dissolution is necessary to legally terminate the existence of a company. Without formally dissolving, the company may continue to incur taxes, filing requirements, and potential penalties. It's a crucial step to ensure that all liabilities and obligations of the business are properly settled.

cards.title: Are there different procedures for different states?
content: Yes, each state has its own specific requirements and procedures for dissolving a business. It's important to follow the guidelines of the state where your business is registered.

cards.title: How long does the dissolution process take?
content: The time frame can vary depending on the state and the complexity of the company's affairs. Typically, it can take several weeks to months.

cards.title: What happens if a company is not formally dissolved?
content: If a company is not formally dissolved, it can continue to accrue taxes and penalties, and the owners might remain liable for certain legal and financial obligations.

cards.title: What are the steps to dissolve a U.S. company owned by a non-resident?
content: There are several stages to follow: 1) Get approval from your company’s board and shareholders; 2) File the Articles of Dissolution with the state where your company is registered; 3) Inform and settle with creditors; 4) File your final tax returns with the IRS and any state tax authorities; 5) Close company bank accounts, cancel business licenses, and wrap up any remaining financial obligations.

paragraphs: Non-residents can open a US business bank account entirely online, but approval depends on documentation rather than travel: a registered US entity, an EIN, a verifiable US business address and a business model the compliance team can follow. Traditional branch banks generally require a personal SSN and an in-person visit, so remote founders use fintech platforms that hold funds at partner banks. Most rejections come from flagged addresses, vague business descriptions or mismatched ownership details rather than from the founder's nationality.

sections.title: Articles of Incorporation vs Articles of Organization: What is the Difference
paragraphs: Articles of organization create an LLC and articles of incorporation create a corporation; they are the same kind of filing for two different entity types. Some states use a different name for the identical document — Delaware and Texas call the LLC version a certificate of formation. The only substantive difference is that articles of incorporation authorise shares, which is why outside investors require a corporation.

sections.title: Why Do You Need a Wyoming Registered Agent for Your LLC?
paragraphs: A Wyoming registered agent is the person or company officially designated to accept legal notices and state correspondence for an LLC at a physical Wyoming street address. Wyoming requires every LLC to name one, and because the agent's address appears on the public record, using a home address cancels out most of the state's privacy advantage. This guide covers eligibility, how commercial agent services compare to acting as your own agent, how to change agents, and what happens if the appointment lapses.

cards.title: Accrual Basis Accounting
content: An accounting method where income and expenses are recorded when they are earned or incurred, regardless of when cash is actually received or paid.

content: Electronic funds transfer system for batch-processing low-cost bank payments in the United States.

cards.title: Administrative Dissolution
content: The involuntary closure of a business by the state due to failure to meet compliance requirements like annual report filings or tax payments.

cards.title: Amendment
content: A formal change made to a company’s original formation documents, filed with the state to update key legal or structural business details, such as name, address, or management.

cards.title: Angel Investor
content: Angel Investor: An individual who invests personal funds into early-stage startups (usually in exchange for equity) often providing mentorship alongside capital.

cards.title: Annual Report
content: A mandatory yearly filing to a U.S. state that updates the company’s information (like directors, officers, address) and confirms it’s in compliance, often accompanied by a fee.

cards.title: Apostille
content: A government-issued certificate that authenticates the validity of a document for use in another country, under the Hague Apostille Convention.

cards.title: Articles of Incorporation
content: A document filed with a U.S. state to legally create a corporation, outlining key details like the company name, address, registered agent, and initial stock structure.

cards.title: Articles of Organization
content: A document filed with a U.S. state to legally create a Limited Liability Company (LLC), outlining company details like name, address, registered agent, and sometimes management structure.

cards.title: Assumed Name (DBA)
content: A registered alternate name a business can use to operate publicly, different from its legal entity name.

cards.title: Audit
content: A formal examination of a company’s financial records to ensure accuracy, transparency, and compliance with tax or reporting standards.

cards.title: Authorized Member
content: An owner of an LLC who has the legal authority to act on behalf of the company. What is an Authorized Member?

cards.title: Authorized Representative
content: A person or organization formally permitted to act on behalf of a company in specific legal or administrative matters.

cards.title: Authorized Shares
content: The maximum number of shares of stock that a corporation is legally allowed to issue, as specified in its Articles (or Certificate) of Incorporation.

cards.title: Balance Sheet
content: A financial statement that provides a snapshot of a company’s financial position at a given moment, listing assets, liabilities, and equity.

cards.title: Bank Reconciliation
content: The process of matching and verifying that a company’s accounting records (cash ledger) align with the bank’s records (bank statements), identifying any differences or errors.

cards.title: Beneficial Owner
content: A beneficial owner is the real person who ultimately owns or controls a company, even if the company is legally held in another name.

cards.title: Beneficial Ownership Information Report
content: A confidential report filed with FinCEN (U.S. Treasury) identifying a company’s beneficial owners (and company applicants), required by the Corporate Transparency Act for most U.S. entities as of 2024.

cards.title: Board of Directors
content: A group of individuals elected by shareholders to govern and oversee a corporation’s management and major decisions, typically including company strategy and executive hiring.

cards.title: Bookkeeping
content: The routine recording and organizing of financial transactions (sales, purchases,payments, receipts) of a business, forming the basis of the accounting system.

cards.title: Business Address
content: The official address a company uses for registration, correspondence, and legal purposes.

cards.title: Business Credit
content: A credit profile tied to your company’s legal entity, separate from your personal credit history.

cards.title: Business Entity
content: The legal structure a company adopts, such as an LLC, corporation, or sole proprietorship.

cards.title: Business License
content: A permit that allows a company to legally operate within a specific city, county, or state.

cards.title: Business-to-Business
content: A type of commerce where transactions occur between two businesses rather than between a business and individual consumers.

cards.title: Business-to-Consumer (B2C)
content: A type of commerce where businesses sell products or services directly to individual consumers for personal use.

cards.title: Bylaws
content: The internal rulebook of a corporation, establishing how the corporation is governed and operated, including the roles of directors/officers, meeting procedures, and voting rights.

cards.title: Capital Contribution
content: The money, property, or services that an owner or investor puts into a company in exchange for ownership (used to fund the business without creating debt).

cards.title: Capital Stock
content: The total number of shares a corporation is authorized to issue, representing ownership in the company (includes both common and preferred stock).

cards.title: Capitalization Table (Cap Table)
content: A detailed record of a company’s ownership structure (showing who owns what percentage of equity, including founders, investors, and option holders).

cards.title: Cash Basis Accounting
content: An accounting method where income and expenses are recorded only when cash is actually received or paid (commonly used by small businesses for its simplicity).

cards.title: Cash Flow
content: The movement of money into and out of a business (tracking how much cash is available to operate, pay expenses, and grow).

cards.title: Cash Flow Statement
content: A financial report that shows how cash moves in and out of a business during a specific period (broken into operating, investing, and financing activities) to measure liquidity and financial health.

cards.title: Certificate of Formation
content: The official legal document that registers an LLC or Corporation with the state (commonly used in Delaware for LLCs); once filed and approved, it legally establishes the business as a recognized entity (equivalent to the Articles of Organization).

cards.title: Certificate of Good Standing
content: An official state-issued document that confirms a company is legally registered, up-to-date with all required filings, and authorized to do business in that state.

cards.title: Certificate of Incorporation
content: The legal document filed with the state to officially form a Corporation; it establishes the company’s legal existence and is equivalent to Articles of Incorporation in most states.

cards.title: Certified Copy
content: An official copy of a business document issued and stamped by the state to confirm it is a true and accurate record from state files (commonly requested for legal, banking, or international use).

cards.title: Certified Public Accountant
content: A licensed accounting professional in the U.S. who is qualified to provide tax, audit, and financial advisory services in compliance with federal and state regulations.

cards.title: Chart of Accounts
content: An organized list of all the financial accounts used by a business to classify income, expenses, assets, liabilities, and equity (forming the foundation of its bookkeeping system).

cards.title: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
content: The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) is the highest-ranking executive in a company, responsible for overall strategy, major corporate decisions, and managing the organization’s operations and resources.

cards.title: Chief Financial Officer (CFO)
content: The Chief Financial Officer (CFO) is the executive responsible for managing a company’s finances, including accounting, budgeting, reporting, and strategic financial planning (often appointed after an LLC or corporation is formed to ensure strong fiscal management and compliance).

cards.title: Chief Marketing Officer (CMO)
content: The Chief Marketing Officer (CMO) is the executive responsible for leading a company’s marketing strategy, brand development, and customer engagement to drive growth and revenue.

cards.title: Chief Operating Officer (COO)
content: The Chief Operating Officer (COO) is the executive responsible for managing a company’s daily operations and ensuring that business plans are effectively executed (often appointed after an LLC or corporation is formed to support growth and efficiency).

cards.title: Chief Technology Officer (CTO)
content: The Chief Technology Officer (CTO) is the executive responsible for overseeing a company’s technology strategy, infrastructure, and innovation, ensuring that technology supports the overall business goals.

cards.title: Compliance
content: The act of meeting all legal, regulatory, and tax obligations required to maintain a business’s good standing and lawful operation in the U.S. What is Compliance?

cards.title: Conversion
content: The legal process of changing a company’s entity type or state of formation (such as converting an LLC to a Corporation or moving a Delaware company to another state) while maintaining business continuity.

cards.title: Copyright
content: A legal right that protects original works of authorship (such as books, music, software, artwork, and videos) by giving the creator exclusive rights to use, reproduce, distribute, and display the work, usually for the creator’s lifetime plus a set number of years.

cards.title: Corporate Resolution
content: An official document used by a corporation’s board of directors or shareholders to record and authorize important decisions or actions taken on behalf of the company.

cards.title: Cost of Goods Sold
content: The direct costs of producing or purchasing the goods a business sells (such as materials, labor, and manufacturing) excluding overhead or operating expenses.

cards.title: Delinquent Status
content: A state-imposed label indicating that a company has failed to meet certain compliance obligations, such as filing annual reports or paying required fees (putting it at risk of penalties or dissolution).

cards.title: Depreciation
content: An accounting method that spreads the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life, reflecting wear and tear and reducing taxable income over time.

cards.title: Direct-to-Consumer (D2C)
content: A business model where a company sells its products or services directly to the end consumer without relying on third-party retailers, wholesalers, or marketplaces.

cards.title: Disregarded Entity
content: A business entity that is separate from its owner legally, but treated as the same person for U.S. federal tax purposes (typically refers to a single-member LLC).

cards.title: Dissolution
content: The official process of legally closing a U.S. business at both the state and federal levels (requiring formal filings to terminate the company’s legal existence and end tax and compliance obligations).

cards.title: Dividend
content: A distribution of a portion of a corporation’s profits to its shareholders, typically in cash (or sometimes stock), usually declared by the board of directors, providing owners a return on their investment.

cards.title: Doing Business As (DBA)
content: A registered trade name a business uses that is different from its legal name (often used for branding, operating multiple lines of business, or selling under a different name).

cards.title: Double Taxation
content: A situation where the same income is taxed twice (first at the corporate level and again at the shareholder level when profits are distributed), most commonly associated with C Corporations.

cards.title: Dropshipping
content: An order fulfillment method where the seller does not keep inventory but transfers customer orders directly to a third-party supplier, who ships the product to the customer.

cards.title: DUNS
content: A unique nine-digit identifier issued by Dun & Bradstreet (D&B) to track a business’s credit and financial history.

cards.title: E-commerce
content: The buying and selling of goods or services via the internet, often through online stores or marketplaces, involving digital marketing, electronic payment systems, and delivery logistics.

cards.title: Effective Date
content: The date on which a legal filing (such as a company formation, amendment, or dissolution) officially takes effect as recognized by the state.

cards.title: Effectively Connected Income (ECI)
content: Income earned by a non-U.S. person or business that is connected to a trade or business in the United States and is therefore subject to U.S. taxation.

cards.title: Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS)
content: A secure U.S. Treasury online system for paying federal taxes electronically. What is The Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS)?

cards.title: Employer Identification Number (EIN)
content: A unique nine-digit number issued by the IRS to identify a business for tax purposes (similar to a Social Security Number and Individual Taxpayer Identification Number but for companies).

cards.title: Engaged in Trade or Business in the United States (ETBUS)
content: A status describing when a non-U.S. person or entity has sufficient business activity in the U.S. to be considered as “doing business” there for tax purposes.

cards.title: Entity Classification Election
content: A formal request made to the IRS to choose how a business entity will be classified for U.S. federal tax purposes, such as being taxed as a corporation, partnership, or disregarded entity.

cards.title: Equity
content: Equity represents an ownership interest in a business, typically expressed as shares or a percentage of ownership, which entitles the holder to a portion of the company’s profits and, in some cases, voting rights.

cards.title: Escrow
content: A financial arrangement where a neutral third party holds funds, assets, or documents on behalf of two or more parties until agreed-upon conditions are met.

cards.title: Expense
content: The cost a business incurs in its day-to-day operations to generate revenue, such as rent, salaries, utilities, and supplies.

cards.title: FATCA (Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act)
content: The Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act, or FATCA, is a U.S. law that requires foreign financial institutions and certain other entities to report information about financial accounts held by U.S. taxpayers or by foreign entities in which U.S. taxpayers hold a substantial ownership interest.

cards.title: Federal Tax Identification Number
content: A Federal Tax Identification Number (most commonly an Employer Identification Number (EIN)) is a unique nine-digit number issued by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to identify a business for federal tax purposes.

cards.title: FinCEN (The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network)
content: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, is a bureau of the U.S. Department of the Treasury responsible for collecting and analyzing financial data to combat money laundering, terrorism financing, and other financial crimes.

cards.title: Foreign Qualification
content: The process by which a business registers to legally operate in a state other than its state of formation, allowing it to conduct activities such as hiring employees, opening offices, or maintaining inventory in that state.

cards.title: Foreign-Owned U.S. Entity
content: A business formed in the United States that is at least 25% owned by a foreign individual, company, or other entity.

cards.title: Franchise Tax
content: Franchise tax is a state-imposed fee that businesses must pay for the privilege of being registered and operating in that state.

cards.title: Freelancer
content: A freelancer is a self-employed individual who offers services to clients on a project or contract basis rather than working as an employee.

cards.title: Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA)
content: Fulfillment by Amazon is a service where Amazon stores, packs, and ships products on behalf of sellers.

cards.title: Good Standing
content: A company’s official status showing it is compliant with all state requirements (such as filings, fees, and taxes) allowing it to legally operate and maintain its rights in that state.

cards.title: Gross Profit
content: Gross profit is the amount a business earns from its revenue after subtracting the direct costs of producing goods or delivering services, but before accounting for operating expenses, taxes, or interest.

cards.title: Income Statement (Profit & Loss)
content: A financial report that summarizes a company’s revenues, costs, and expenses over a specific period, showing whether the business made a profit or incurred a loss.

cards.title: Incorporator
content: For corporations, the Incorporator is the person or entity responsible for preparing, signing, and filing the Articles of Incorporation with the state to legally form the company (similar to how an Organizer performs this role for an LLC).

cards.title: Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
content: An Individual Taxpayer Identification Number issued by the IRS to non-U.S. residents and others who are not eligible for a Social Security Number, used primarily for federal tax purposes.

cards.title: Intellectual Property Rights (IP Rights)
content: The legal rights that protect creations of the mind, such as inventions, designs, brands, and creative works, and that give their owners exclusive control over how they are used and distributed.

cards.title: Intent to Use (ITU)
content: A trademark application basis in which the applicant declares that they have a genuine plan to use the mark in commerce in the near future, but have not yet started selling goods or services under that mark.

cards.title: Internal Revenue Service
content: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) is the U.S. federal agency responsible for administering and enforcing tax laws, including the collection of taxes and processing of tax returns.

cards.title: Invoice
content: An invoice is a commercial document issued by a seller to a buyer that lists goods or services provided, their quantities, prices, and payment terms.

cards.title: Joint Venture (JV)
content: A business arrangement in which two or more parties agree to combine resources to accomplish a specific project or business activity while remaining separate legal entities.

cards.title: KYC (Know Your Customer)
content: A verification process that businesses, especially financial institutions, use to confirm the identity of their clients to prevent fraud, money laundering, and other illegal activities.

cards.title: Liability
content: A legal obligation or debt a business or individual owes, usually as a result of contracts, laws, or wrongful acts (can include money owed, duties to perform, or responsibility for damages).

cards.title: Limited Partnership (LP)
content: A business structure that includes at least one general partner who manages the business and assumes unlimited liability, and one or more limited partners who contribute capital but have limited liability and no active management role.

cards.title: Mail Forwarding
content: A service that receives mail on behalf of a business or individual at a designated address and then forwards it to another location, often used by businesses without a physical U.S. office to maintain a U.S. mailing address.

cards.title: Manager (LLC)
content: An individual or entity appointed to handle the day-to-day operations and decision-making of a Limited Liability Company (LLC) when the business is structured as manager-managed instead of member-managed.

cards.title: Manager-Managed LLC
content: A Limited Liability Company in which the owners, called members, appoint one or more managers to run the day-to-day operations instead of managing the business themselves.

cards.title: Member (LLC)
content: An owner of a Limited Liability Company (LLC) who holds a percentage of the business, known as a membership interest, and has certain rights to profits, voting, and participation in the company’s management.

cards.title: Member-Managed LLC
content: A Limited Liability Company in which all owners, called members, are directly involved in running the day-to-day operations and making business decisions.

cards.title: Multi-Member LLC
content: A Limited Liability Company with two or more owners, called members, who share in the ownership, management, and profits of the business.

cards.title: Notice of Allowance (NoA)
content: A formal notification from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) indicating that a trademark application has passed the examination process and will be allowed for registration once additional requirements are met, usually proof of actual use in commerce.

cards.title: NRA (Non-Resident Alien)
content: An individual who is not a U.S. citizen and does not meet the IRS substantial presence or green card test for tax residency.

cards.title: Office Action
content: A formal communication from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) to a trademark or patent applicant, outlining issues or requirements that must be addressed before the application can proceed toward approval.

cards.title: Officer
content: An individual appointed by a corporation or LLC to manage day-to-day operations and carry out the decisions of the owners or board of directors.

cards.title: Operating Agreement
content: A legal document that outlines the ownership, structure, and operating rules of an LLC.

cards.title: Operating Income
content: The profit a business earns from its core operations after subtracting operating expenses from gross profit, without including income from non-operational activities.

cards.title: Option Pool
content: A set number of company shares reserved for future issuance to employees, advisors, or consultants as part of equity-based compensation plans.

cards.title: Out-of-State Registration
content: The process of registering an existing company to legally operate in a state other than the one where it was originally formed.

cards.title: Outstanding Shares
content: The total number of a company’s shares of stock that are currently owned by all shareholders, including those held by institutional investors and company insiders.

cards.title: Overhead Costs
content: Ongoing business expenses that are not directly tied to producing goods or services but are necessary to keep the business running.

cards.title: Owner’s Draw
content: Money taken out of a business by the owner for personal use, typically in businesses like sole proprietorships, partnerships, or LLCs taxed as pass-through entities.

cards.title: Par Value
content: The nominal or face value assigned to a share of stock by a corporation at the time it is authorized, as stated in the company’s formation documents.

cards.title: Partnership
content: A business structure where two or more individuals or entities agree to operate a business together, sharing profits, losses, and management responsibilities according to an agreed arrangement.

cards.title: Pass-Through Taxation
content: A tax structure (also called flow-through taxation) where business income “passes through” to the owners’ personal tax returns, avoiding corporate-level income tax and the double taxation faced by C corporations.

cards.title: Payroll Tax
content: Taxes that employers are required to withhold from employees’ wages and pay to government agencies, along with employer-paid contributions, to fund programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance.

cards.title: President
content: The top executive officer in a corporation responsible for overseeing the company’s overall operations, executing strategic plans, and ensuring that business objectives set by the board of directors are met.

cards.title: Profit Margin
content: A percentage that shows how much profit a business makes for every dollar of revenue after covering its costs.

cards.title: Qualified Business Income
content: Net business income earned from a U.S. pass-through entity that may be eligible for a 20% federal tax deduction under Section 199A of the U.S. Tax Code.

cards.title: Quarterly Estimated Taxes
content: Periodic tax payments made to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and, in some cases, state tax authorities to cover income that is not subject to withholding, such as self-employment income, business profits, dividends, or rental income.

cards.title: Quarterly Taxes
content: Quarterly taxes are estimated tax payments made four times a year to the IRS (and sometimes state tax agencies) to cover income and self-employment taxes as you earn income, rather than waiting until the end of the year.

cards.title: Registered Agent
content: An individual or company officially appointed to receive a business’s legal documents, government notices, tax forms, and service of process (lawsuits) on its behalf, ensuring the business stays informed and compliant with state requirements.

cards.title: Reinstatement
content: The process of restoring a business entity that has been administratively dissolved (by bringing it back into good standing with the state through filings and payment of fees).

cards.title: Resale Certificate
content: A document that allows a business to purchase goods tax-free if those goods are intended for resale; used to avoid paying sales tax on inventory purchases.

cards.title: Revenue
content: The total amount of money a business earns from selling goods or services before any expenses are deducted.

cards.title: Routing Number
content: A routing number is a unique nine-digit code used in the U.S. banking system to identify the specific financial institution where a bank account is held.

cards.title: S Corporation (S-Corp)
content: A U.S. corporation that has elected to be taxed as a pass-through entity, allowing profits and losses to flow directly to shareholders, avoiding double taxation at the federal level.

cards.title: SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity)
content: A startup investment agreement where an investor provides capital in exchange for the right to receive equity in a future priced round (commonly used in early-stage fundraising).

cards.title: Sales Tax
content: A state-level tax charged on the sale of goods or certain services, collected from customers and remitted to the state by the seller.

cards.title: Schedule K-1
content: A U.S. tax form used by partnerships and certain LLCs or S corporations to report each owner’s share of the business’s income, deductions, and credits to the IRS and to the owner.

cards.title: Secretary
content: A corporate officer responsible for maintaining a company’s official records, preparing and keeping meeting minutes, and ensuring compliance with legal and reporting requirements.

cards.title: Secretary of State
content: The Secretary of State (SOS) is the state government office responsible for registering and maintaining official records for businesses, such as LLCs and corporations, and ensuring they remain in compliance with state requirements.

cards.title: Share (Stock)
content: A unit of ownership in a corporation, representing a claim on the company’s assets and earnings (commonly issued to founders, investors, or employees).

cards.title: Shareholder
content: An individual or entity that owns shares in a corporation, giving them a financial interest in the company and certain rights, such as voting or receiving dividends.

cards.title: Shareholder Agreement
content: A private contract between a corporation’s shareholders that outlines their rights, responsibilities, and rules on how the company will be owned and operated.

cards.title: Single-Member LLC (SMLLC)
content: A Limited Liability Company with only one owner (member). It offers liability protection and flexible taxation (usually treated as a “disregarded entity” for U.S. tax purposes by default).

cards.title: Social Security Number (SSN)
content: A 9-digit identification number issued by the U.S. government to citizens and eligible residents (primarily used for taxation, employment, and government benefits).

cards.title: Sole Proprietorship
content: A sole proprietorship is the simplest type of business structure in the U.S., owned and operated by one person.

cards.title: Specimen (Trademark Filing)
content: A real-world example showing how a trademark is actually used in commerce to identify and distinguish goods or services.

cards.title: Startup
content: A newly founded business, typically designed to scale quickly by solving a problem with an innovative product, service, or business model (often in tech or high-growth industries).

cards.title: State Income Tax
content: State income tax is a tax imposed by individual U.S. states on income earned within their borders.

cards.title: Statement of Information
content: A Statement of Information is a mandatory filing that keeps a U.S. state’s records about your company up to date, including details like business addresses, owners, and officers.

cards.title: Statement of Use
content: A Statement of Use (SOU) is a filing submitted to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) in an “Intent to Use” trademark application to prove that the trademark is now being used in U.S. commerce.

cards.title: Tax Nexus
content: A legal connection between a business and a U.S. state that requires the business to collect and remit taxes in that state.

cards.title: Tax Treaty
content: A formal agreement between two countries that reduces or eliminates double taxation on income earned across borders.

cards.title: TIN (Taxpayer Identification Number)
content: A unique number (such as the EIN, ITIN, or SSN) used by the IRS to identify individuals and businesses for tax purposes in the United States.

cards.title: Trade Name
content: A Trade Name is a name that a business uses publicly that is different from its legal name (also known as a “Doing Business As” (DBA) name).

cards.title: Trademark
content: A trademark is a word, phrase, symbol, design, or combination of these that identifies and distinguishes the source of goods or services, protecting a brand’s identity in the marketplace.

cards.title: Treasurer
content: A treasurer is a corporate officer responsible for managing a company’s financial assets, overseeing budgets, and ensuring accurate financial reporting.

cards.title: Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO)
content: The individual who ultimately owns or controls a business, even if the business is held through other companies, nominees, or intermediaries.

cards.title: Use Tax
content: A tax imposed by U.S. states on goods purchased without paying sales tax and later used, stored, or consumed within the state.

cards.title: USPS 1583
content: A form required by the United States Postal Service that authorizes a Commercial Mail Receiving Agency (CMRA), such as a virtual mailbox or mail forwarding service, to receive and handle mail on behalf of an individual or business.

cards.title: Valuation Cap
content: A clause in a SAFE or convertible note that sets the maximum company valuation at which an investor’s investment will convert into equity (designed to protect early investors from excessive dilution in future funding rounds).

cards.title: Vendor
content: An individual or company that sells goods or services to another business or customer; often used in business-to-business (B2B) transactions and vendor agreements.

cards.title: Venture Capital
content: A type of private equity financing provided by investors to early-stage, high-growth startups in exchange for equity (commonly used to fund innovation, scale operations, and enter new markets).

cards.title: Vesting
content: The process by which someone earns ownership of shares or benefits (such as stock options or equity) over time, rather than receiving them all at once.

cards.title: Vice President (VP)
content: A corporate officer responsible for overseeing specific areas of a company’s operations or management, often acting as second-in-command to the President or CEO.

cards.title: Virtual Office
content: A service that provides a business with a U.S. mailing address and other office-like functions (such as mail handling and business presence) without renting physical office space; commonly used by remote teams and…

cards.title: Void Status
content: A legal status assigned by a state when a business entity has failed to meet certain compliance requirements, resulting in the loss of its legal rights and good standing.

cards.title: Voting Rights
content: The legal right of a shareholder or member to vote on key company matters, such as electing directors or approving major decisions (based on the type and number of shares or ownership held).

cards.title: W-8BEN / W-8BEN-E
content: IRS forms used by non-U.S. individuals (W-8BEN) and entities (W-8BEN-E) to certify their foreign status and claim tax treaty benefits for income earned from U.S. sources.

cards.title: W-9
content: An IRS form used by U.S. persons and entities to provide their Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) to another party, usually for tax reporting purposes.

cards.title: Wire Transfer
content: An electronic transfer of funds between banks (used for sending money quickly and securely, especially across international borders or for large transactions).

cards.title: Withholding Agent
content: ​​A person or company responsible for withholding U.S. taxes from payments made to foreign individuals or businesses and remitting them to the IRS.

cards.title: Withholding Tax
content: A tax withheld at the source of income (often by the payer) before the payment is made to the recipient.

cards.title: Working Capital
content: The difference between a company’s current assets (cash, accounts receivable, inventory) and current liabilities (accounts payable, short-term loans, accrued expenses).

cards.title: Year-End
content: The last day of a company’s accounting year (used to close the books, prepare financial reports, and file taxes).

cards.title: Zero Balance Account (ZBA)
content: A type of business bank account that automatically transfers all funds to or from a central account at the end of each business day, leaving the balance at zero.

7. EUROPEAN ECONOMIC AREA AND UNITED KINGDOM PRIVACY LAW
Your Rights and Choices Under the GDPR

Right of Access

Right to Rectification

Right to Restrict Processing

Right to Data Portability

Right to Object

Right not to be Subjected to Automated Individual Decision-Making

Right to File a Complaint

Right to Seek Compensation for Damages

Do Not Sell My Personal Information

We do share Personal Information with Third Parties that we work with, including for the purpose of helping us market or advertise our products and Services to you with regard to your prior consent whenever required by applicable law. You can find more details about our practices in our Policy, set forth under the "Interest-based Advertising" section.

If you wish to opt out of the use of your Personal Information for interest-based advertising purposes and these potential Sales of Data as defined under the CCPA, you may do so by following the instructions below;

Some internet browsers have enabled 'Do Not Track' (DNT) features, which send out a signal (called the DNT signal) to the websites that you visit indicating that you do not wish to be tracked. If you are visiting such websites, you can set your preferences in your web browser to inform websites that you do not want to be tracked. You can enable or disable DNT by visiting the preferences or settings page of your web browser.
California Privacy Rights for Minor Users (California Business and Professions Code Section 22581)

We do not knowingly process the Personal Information of California residents under the age of 18 without the approval of their legal guardian. Your Personal Information may be disclosed in response to inquiries or requests from government authorities or to respond to judicial processes within the countries in which we operate.
12.INTERNATIONAL DATA TRANSFERS

Your Personal Information will be processed by us in the European Economic Area (“EEA”), Türkiye, and the USA. Personal information may be stored and processed in any country where we have operations or where we engage service providers. Those countries may have data protection rules that are different from those of your country. In certain circumstances, courts, law enforcement agencies, regulatory agencies, or security authorities in those other countries may be entitled to access your Personal Information.

15.LINKS TO OTHER WEBSITES

sections.title: 3. About Cookies
paragraphs: Cookies are small pieces of information, normally consisting of just letters and numbers, which online services provide when users visit them. Software on the user’s device (for example a web browser) can store cookies and send them back to the Platform next time they visit.

cards.title: According Storage Period:
content: Persistent Cookies will be stored by a web browser and remain valid until a set expiry date unless the user deletes it,
Session Cookies will expire at the end of a user’s session, upon closure of the Platform.

cards.title: According to the Party:
content: First-party cookies are set directly by the Platform (the URL displayed in the browser address bar).
Third-party cookies are set by another domain, such as service providers, for purposes such as advertising or analytics.

cards.title: According to the Purpose:
content: Strictly necessary / essential cookies are required for the proper functioning of the Platform and the provision of services, as well as access to the Platform’s secure areas. Without enabling these cookies, the Platform would not be able to work properly.
Functional cookies are used on Platform in order to store information about users’ preferences and to personalize their experience.
Performance and analytics cookies are used in order to collect and report information about the use and performance of the Platform and the services provided.

Marketing and targeted advertising cookies are used in order to properly display relevant advertising to users by tracking their online activity and establishing a profile suitable for their interests and needs.

Other cookies do not necessarily fall into the typical categories such as functional, performance, or advertising cookies. They may include cookies used for purposes that are specific to the individual site’s needs or technology.

cards.title: Similar Technologies:
content: Cookies are not the sole method for identifying or monitoring visitors on a Platform. Occasionally, we may employ other similar technologies, such as web beacons (sometimes referred to as “tracking pixels” or “clear gifs”). These are small image files containing a unique identifier which allows us to detect visits to our application. This enables us to track user traffic patterns from one page to another within our app, facilitate the use or communication of cookies, determine if you accessed our app through an online advertisement on a third-party app, enhance app performance, and evaluate the effectiveness of email marketing campaigns. In most cases, these technologies rely on cookies for their operation, so rejecting cookies may impede their functionality.

sections.title: Legal Basis and Processing Purposes for Cookie Usage

cards.title: 4.1 Strictly Necessary / Essential Cookies
content: These cookies are necessary for the functioning of the website. They ensure the proper technical functioning and security of the website, enable essential features, and provide the services explicitly requested by you.

cards.title: 4.2 Functional Cookies
content: These cookies enable us to enhance the functionality and personalization of our website by remembering choices you make (such as your user name, language, or the region you are in). Although these cookies contribute to a better user experience, they are not essential for the use of the site.

cards.title: 4.3 Analytical/Performance Cookies
content: These cookies help us to understand how visitors interact with our website by providing information about the areas visited, the time spent on the site, and any issues encountered, such as error messages. This helps us to improve the performance of our website.

cards.title: 4.4 Advertising/Marketing Cookies
content: These cookies are used to deliver advertisements more relevant to you and your interests. They are also used to limit the number of times you see an advertisement as well as help measure the effectiveness of the advertising campaign.
Legal Basis: The processing of these cookies is strictly based on your explicit consent.

sections.title: Objectives for Processing Personal Data through Cookies

cards.title: 5.1 Strictly Necessary / Essential Cookies
content: The primary objective for using essential cookies is to enable fundamental functions such as site navigation and access to secure areas of the website. Without these cookies, key aspects of the website, including security and service continuity, cannot function properly. These cookies ensure that the website operates efficiently and securely, providing a base level of user experience that is crucial for the operation of the site.

cards.title: 5.2 Functional Cookies
content: Functional cookies are used with the objective to enhance user experience on our website. By remembering users’ settings and preferences (e.g., language selection, region, or login status), these cookies allow us to offer more personalized and convenient features. They facilitate better user interaction with the website, adapting the website’s environment to each user’s specifications and preferences to make their interaction smoother and more intuitive.

cards.title: 5.3 Analytical/Performance
content: Cookies The objective of using analytical/performance cookies is to collect data that helps us understand how visitors use our website. This involves tracking the number of visitors, the most frequently visited pages, and any errors experienced. Such data is crucial for analyzing website performance and usability, allowing us to identify popular features and areas for improvement. Ultimately, this leads to optimized website performance that aligns with user behaviors and preferences, enhancing overall user satisfaction.

cards.title: 5.4 Advertising/Marketing Cookies
content: The use of advertising/marketing cookies aims to provide targeted advertising tailored to each user. These cookies track browsing habits and are used to display advertisements that are more relevant to the individual user. Additionally, they help in managing the efficiency of these advertising campaigns. The objective is to engage users with ads that are pertinent to their interests, thereby increasing the effectiveness of promotional content and contributing to better marketing strategies.
